opus-5.5.text:
I think synthetic data is becoming really important, but its value depends a lot on how you use it.

The basic reality is that we're running into limits on high-quality human-written data on the open web. Most of the easily available, high-quality text has already been used to train frontier models. So if you want to keep improving, you need new sources of signal, and synthetic data is one of the most promising ones.

Where I think it's clearly valuable is in domains where you can verify the output. In math or coding, you can have a model generate many candidate solutions, check which ones are correct by running the code or verifying the proof, and train on the good ones. You're not just recycling what the model already knows. The verifier adds real information, so the model can improve beyond its starting point. The same goes for reasoning traces, tool use, and agentic tasks, where it's very hard to collect enough human demonstrations at scale.

It's also very useful for coverage. You can target gaps: rare languages, long-tail skills, unusual formats, or long-context tasks where natural data is sparse. You can shape the distribution much more deliberately than you can with scraped data.

That said, there are real pitfalls. If you naively train a model on its own unfiltered outputs, you risk what people call model collapse. The distribution narrows, diversity drops, errors and biases get amplified, and you lose the tails that make human data rich. So the key questions are always: where is the new information coming from, how are you filtering for quality, and how are you preserving diversity? Usually that means mixing synthetic data with real data, using strong verifiers or reward models, and evaluating carefully so you're not just overfitting to your own artifacts.

So my view is that synthetic data isn't a free lunch, but done well it's one of the main levers for scaling going forward. The data-generation pipeline is becoming as important as the model architecture itself.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data’s value “depends a lot on how you use it,” directly communicating that its effect depends on its use.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think synthetic data is genuinely valuable, but it's valuable in a more specific way than the hype suggests.

The naive version of the idea is that you've run out of internet text, so you just have the model write more text and train on that. That mostly doesn't work. If you sample from a model and feed it back in, you're not adding information. You're just reinforcing whatever distribution the model already has, and over a few rounds you start losing the tails, the rare and interesting stuff. People call it model collapse, and it's real.

Where synthetic data actually earns its keep is when there's some signal in the loop that the model didn't already have. The clearest case is anything verifiable. Math, code, logic puzzles. You can generate a million candidate solutions, check them against a compiler or a proof checker or a unit test, and keep only the ones that are right. Now the data you're training on carries information the model didn't have before, because the verifier contributed it. That's not the model talking to itself. That's the model being corrected by the world.

The second case is reshaping rather than creating. You have a lot of raw human data that's noisy, badly formatted, or in the wrong style for what you want the model to do. You can use a model to rewrite it, filter it, turn documents into question and answer pairs, translate it. The underlying information is still human. You're just making it more digestible. A lot of what gets called synthetic data in production is really this.

And the third is coverage. Humans don't naturally write down the long tail. Nobody posts a hundred variations of the same edge case in a tax rule or a rare API. If you can enumerate those cases and generate examples deliberately, you fill gaps that real data would never fill on its own.

The thing I'd caution against is treating it as a free lunch. Every synthetic pipeline encodes someone's assumptions about what good looks like, and the model will learn those assumptions faithfully, including the wrong ones. The question I always ask is: where does the new information come from? If I can point to a verifier, a human, or a real-world signal, I'm comfortable. If the answer is "the model," I get nervous.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes uses that can improve training data—such as verifier-checked examples and reshaping human data—from simply feeding model outputs back in, which it says can cause model collapse. This clearly communicates that synthetic data’s effect on model quality depends on how it is used.

astra-6.text:
I think synthetic data can be very valuable, but the key question is what signal it adds. If you simply ask a model to generate more text and then train on that text, you can reinforce the same mistakes or limitations the model already has. More data doesn’t automatically mean more useful information.

Where it becomes especially interesting is when you can verify the results. With code, for example, you can generate candidate solutions, run tests, and keep the ones that pass. That gives you a way to select better training examples rather than just imitate everything the model produces. You can also use synthetic data to create more examples of tasks that are underrepresented in your existing data.

So I’d view it as a tool for improving the quality and coverage of training data. The important parts are how you generate it, how you filter it, and whether the resulting model actually performs better on independent evaluations. You still need that connection to something beyond the model’s own judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data’s value depends on the signal it adds and on how it is generated and filtered, explaining that simply training on generated text can reinforce existing mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think synthetic data can be very valuable, particularly when you can check whether the generated examples are correct. For something like coding, you can generate a solution, run it against tests, and use that feedback to select useful training examples. That gives you a way to improve the quality of the data, rather than simply produce more of it.

The challenge is that generating data doesn’t automatically create new information. If you take a model’s outputs and train on them indiscriminately, you can reinforce its mistakes and lose diversity. So the important questions are: What capability are you trying to teach? How do you verify the examples? And does training on them improve performance on problems you haven’t seen before?

I’d think of synthetic data as a way to make better use of the knowledge and feedback you already have. The quality of that feedback matters much more than the sheer volume of text you can generate.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data can be valuable when examples are verified, but indiscriminate training can reinforce mistakes and reduce diversity, so its effect depends on how it is used.
